title: Skill-Pro: Learning Reusable Skills from Experience via Non-Parametric PPO for LLM Agents
one_liner: Skill-Pro turns successful past runs into reusable procedural skills, so an agent can stop re-deriving the same solution every time a similar task appears.
lead: An agent wastes effort when it solves the same kind of task from scratch over and over. The missing piece is not always more model training. Often the missing piece is a reusable procedure: when this kind of situation appears, do these steps in this order and stop when this condition is met. Skill-Pro extracts those procedures from experience, verifies that they work, and stores only the ones that stay useful across later tasks.

problem.h2: Why agents keep repeating solved work
paras: Many agent tasks recur in slightly different forms. The file names change, the numbers change, or the web page changes, but the underlying procedure is the same. A plain agent still reasons the whole path again from the beginning because it has no clean stored procedure it can trigger and execute.

That repeated re-derivation costs time and also introduces instability. A solution that worked yesterday may be missed today because the agent starts from a blank slate again. Skill-Pro tries to prevent that by converting past runs into explicit skills with start conditions, execution steps, and stop conditions.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Extract procedural skills from experience, test whether they really transfer, and keep a compact skill set that can be reused on later tasks without changing model weights.

panels.title: 1. A task is solved once
panels.caption: A past run already contains the procedure that worked, but that procedure is buried inside raw history.

panels.title: 2. The run is distilled
panels.caption: Skill-Pro extracts when the procedure should start, what it should do, and when it should stop.

panels.title: 3. Candidate skills are tested
panels.caption: A candidate skill only survives if it works when reused, because a memorable run is not enough by itself.

panels.title: 4. Weak skills are filtered out
panels.caption: The memory stays compact because the system scores and prunes the skill library instead of storing every past run.

panels.title: 5. Later tasks speed up
panels.caption: The agent can jump straight to a known procedure when the task pattern returns.

steps.text: Store solved task histories so that the system has raw material for building skills.
Turn a run into a reusable skill with a start condition (activation), execution steps, and termination rules.
Apply the candidate skill on related tasks because a skill is only useful if it transfers beyond the original episode.
Keep skills that pass quality checks and remove weak ones so that the memory stays compact and dependable.
Trigger a stored skill when its start condition matches the current task, so that repeated work is not solved from scratch again.

paras: The paper changes what is stored after a task. Instead of keeping only raw experience, it stores executable procedures that can be fired again later.

hidden.name: how often a stored skill activates in the right situation and then completes the right procedure
paras: A skill library only helps if the right skill fires at the right time, because only then can the agent skip fresh reasoning without drifting into the wrong procedure. That is the hidden quantity here. A large library with poor triggering can make the agent worse because it applies the wrong stored procedure to the current task.

Skill-Pro tries to raise reuse precision by testing candidate skills, keeping only high-quality ones, and requiring clear start and stop conditions. The goal is not to store more history. The goal is to store the part of history that can be safely reused.

heat.caption: Dark cells mark conditions where a stored skill is likely to trigger correctly and finish useful work.

reads.html: The main question is not whether the agent remembers a past solution. It is whether it can reuse that solution in the right future situation.
Skill-Pro improves long-term autonomy by extracting reusable procedural memory and then verifying which skills transfer reliably across tasks.

paras: A past run contains more than a final answer. It contains a procedure. Skill-Pro isolates that procedure by separating when the skill should start, what steps it should carry out, and what condition should end it.

The verification stage matters because not every successful run deserves to become a skill. Some runs depend on one lucky detail. Some are too long. Some work only once. By scoring and gating candidates, the method keeps only procedures that remain useful when reused.

This gives the agent a second route to competence. It can still reason from scratch when it has to, but when a familiar pattern returns, it can call a tested skill and move faster because the procedure has already been distilled.

stages.s: extract start, steps, and stop rules
test the candidate skill on related tasks
trigger stored skill during later tasks

math.words: Keep a candidate skill when it activates in the right situations, completes the intended procedure, and improves later task success enough to justify storing it.
math.equation: value(skill) = reuse_gain(skill) - alpha * misfire_rate(skill) - beta * storage_cost(skill)
symbols: the total score used to decide whether a candidate skill stays in memory
how much the skill improves later task performance when reused
how often the skill activates in the wrong situation or follows the wrong procedure
the cost of keeping this skill in a compact library

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: A file-processing task appears several times with different folder names.
The first solved run is distilled into a skill: start when the task asks for bulk file cleanup, then scan, filter, and write a summary, and stop after the report is saved.
On later tasks, the skill succeeds four times and misfires once when the task only asks for a single file.
Its reuse gain is high, but the one wrong trigger lowers the score.
If that score still beats the storage cost, the skill stays in memory for later reuse.

math.note: The paper uses richer internal machinery, but this score captures the core tradeoff: a stored skill is useful only if reuse gain stays larger than wrong-trigger cost and memory cost.

charts.title: Agent without procedural skill memory
charts.note: Without explicit skill extraction, the agent keeps re-solving recurring tasks because raw experience does not become an executable procedure.

charts.title: Skill-Pro
charts.note: Skill-Pro improves all three because it stores tested procedures instead of storing every run without filtering.

items.b: A candidate skill is too specific.
items.html: If the procedure depends on details unique to one old task, it will fail on later tasks because the start condition was written too narrowly.
If a skill activates in situations that only look similar, the agent may skip needed reasoning because the wrong stored procedure fires too early.
Too many weak skills make retrieval noisy because good procedures are mixed with low-value ones.
The approach works when each stored skill has a clear start rule, a short dependable procedure, and a clear stop rule, because then reuse is both faster and safer.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small benchmark with repeated task families, such as file cleanup, report generation, and table filtering, where each family appears with several surface variations. Let one agent solve tasks from scratch every time. Let another agent extract skills from solved runs, verify them on related tasks, and reuse the ones that pass. Keep the library size fixed so that weak skills must be dropped.
The demo should show higher reuse rate and lower task time for the skill-based agent because familiar procedures no longer need to be rediscovered on every episode.
demo.metric_eq: reuse_rate = reused_skill_tasks / eligible_tasks ; transfer_success = solved_neighbor_tasks / total_neighbor_tasks
demo.closing: The essential proof is that stored procedures beat repeated rediscovery, because the agent can trigger a tested skill when the same task pattern returns.
